title: Two different fractions in a density-label experiment
stem:
Bacteria initially contain only heavy-isotope DNA. After transfer to light-isotope medium, all DNA is copied once per generation. The figure shows heavy DNA initially, a single intermediate band after generation 1, and intermediate plus light bands after generation 2. Every original heavy strand remains intact; newly made strands contain only light isotope. Assume equal DNA lengths, no degradation and complete replication.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the generation-1 result rejects the simple conservative model and how generation 2 distinguishes semiconservative from the simple dispersive model.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: At generation 3, calculate the fraction of double-stranded molecules that still contain heavy material and the fraction of all DNA strands that are heavy.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why equal band widths in the schematic do not justify a 1:1 amount ratio at generation 3.

steps.text: Conservative copying predicts separate unchanged heavy and entirely light molecules after one generation, rather than one intermediate band.
Semiconservative copying retains one old strand in each first-generation molecule; subsequent copying produces both hybrid and entirely light molecules.
Simple dispersive copying predicts mixtures of old/new material within all molecules, with a shifting intermediate band rather than a distinct entirely light band.
Starting from one molecule, there are eight double-stranded molecules and sixteen strands after three generations.
Two molecules contain an original heavy strand: 2/8 = 1/4 are hybrid.
Only the two original strands are heavy: 2/16 = 1/8 of strands are heavy.
The drawing specifies band positions, not calibrated amounts. Semiconservative tracking predicts a 1:3 hybrid:light molecule ratio at generation 3.

title: A matching DNA profile is evidence with a denominator
stem:
An unknown DNA sample U and reference samples A and B are profiled at two markers. All bands are resolved, and both alleles at each marker are represented by the shown pattern; U and A match at both markers, while B differs. In the relevant reference population, the two matching marker-genotype frequencies are 0.080 and 0.050. For this calculation assume independence between markers, a single-source sample and error-free typing.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare the references with U and calculate the probability that a randomly selected unrelated individual from the stated population matches both markers.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Evaluate the statement “there is therefore a 99.6% probability that A is the source”.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how adding informative independent markers changes evidential strength, and give a reason independence must be checked.

steps.text: A is consistent with all shown U bands; B is excluded under the stated error-free single-source assumptions.
Multiply the genotype-match frequencies because independence is supplied.
Random-match probability = 0.080 × 0.050 = 0.00400, or 0.400%.
A random-match probability concerns an unrelated individual’s profile, not the probability of source identity conditional on a match.
The source conclusion also depends on the number of possible sources, prior/contextual evidence and contamination or typing risks.
Further marker-match frequencies below one reduce the combined random-match probability if genuinely independent.
Linked or population-associated markers may not be independent; multiplying marginal frequencies without checking can overstate the strength of a match.

title: PCR amplification and a contaminated control
stem:
A PCR begins with four double-stranded target molecules. For cycles 1–10 each molecule produces one additional copy per cycle. In cycles 11–15 the expected fractional increase per cycle is 0.80, so multiply by 1.80 per cycle. Treat this as an expected-value model. A separate gel shows a target-sized band in the sample S, positive control P and no-template control N.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the expected target-molecule count after cycle 15 and its fraction of the perfect-doubling prediction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the sample band cannot yet be accepted as reliable evidence that the original sample contained the target.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Relate the roles of heat, primers and Taq polymerase to amplification.

steps.text: After cycle 10 there are 4 × 2¹⁰ = 4096 molecules.
After cycle 15 the expected count is 4096 × 1.80⁵ ≈ 7.74 × 10⁴ molecules.
Perfect doubling gives 4 × 2¹⁵ = 131072; expected yield is (1.80/2)⁵ = 59.0% of this.
The no-template control should not amplify target DNA; its band indicates contamination or another source of false amplification.
A positive sample band can then arise from the same problem. Repeat with clean reagents and contamination controls before accepting the result.
Heating separates the DNA strands; cooling allows primers to pair with target regions.
Taq extends from paired primers and tolerates repeated high-temperature strand-separation cycles; primers help define which region is amplified.

title: A substitution can preserve sequence or change a side chain
stem:
The reference mRNA segment and two single-base variants are shown. Use the supplied code: AUG = methionine, GAA/GAG = glutamate, UUU = phenylalanine, UUA = leucine and UGA = stop. Read the displayed mRNA left to right. No regulatory or splicing effects are included in this model.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the amino-acid sequence represented by each segment and state why the stop codon is not an additional amino acid.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how X illustrates degeneracy and why this does not establish that every substitution is harmless.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The three-amino-acid product is treated as a complete short peptide in this model. State how many peptide bonds form and explain the distinction between codon and anticodon.

steps.text: Reference: Met–Glu–Phe; X: Met–Glu–Phe; Y: Met–Glu–Leu.
A stop codon signals termination and does not encode an amino acid.
Two different codons, GAA and GAG, encode the same amino acid in the supplied code, so X preserves the primary sequence.
Other substitutions can change an amino acid or create/remove a stop; Y changes phenylalanine to leucine. Phenotypic effects depend on the affected protein region.
Two peptide bonds connect three amino acids.
A codon is an mRNA triplet; a complementary tRNA anticodon helps match an amino acid to a sense codon. A stop is not decoded by an amino-acid-carrying tRNA.

title: A mosaic mutation does not have a fixed one-half transmission risk
stem:
In a model diploid animal, an early mutation occurs in lineage B, which later contributes to both body tissues and gametes. Lineage A contributes only to body tissues. Testing shows the mutation in 20.0% of mature gametes. Assume fertilizations independently sample those gametes, the other parent lacks the mutation, and offspring viability is unaffected.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the mutation can be inherited even if many body cells lack it, and why a mutation restricted to A would have a different consequence.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the probability that at least one of four offspring inherits the mutation. Explain why automatically using a 1/2 gamete probability is unjustified.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the inference that the mutation occurred because the animal needed a new trait.

steps.text: B contributes to the germline, so some gametes can carry the mutation despite mosaic body tissues.
A contributes only to somatic tissues in the model, so a mutation confined to A would not be transmitted through these gametes.
The probability that none inherits it is (1−0.200)⁴.
At least one inherits it with probability 1−0.800⁴ = 0.5904, or 59.04%.
The measured gamete fraction is 20%, rather than the uniform heterozygous germline assumed by a simple 1:1 segregation model.
The lineage and transmission data concern where a mutation arose and how it is inherited; they do not show a need-directed origin.
Mutations supply new variation; selection can subsequently alter the frequency of heritable variants.

title: Meiotic stage inferred from all four products
stem:
A species has 2n = 6. The figure shows chromosome counts in all four products from one meiosis in each of two cells. X produces 4, 4, 2, 2; Y produces 4, 2, 3, 3. In each case one nondisjunction event affects a single chromosome pair or its sister chromatids. Assume all products are recovered and no chromosome is gained or lost by another process.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the most consistent stage of nondisjunction in X and Y, explaining the complete pattern rather than a single abnormal product.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: If each product fertilizes a normal gamete, determine the resulting chromosome counts and the fraction of zygotes with the normal count in each case.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why copying DNA before meiosis does not change 2n from 6 to 12.

steps.text: X is consistent with meiosis I nondisjunction; both homologues enter one first-division cell and neither enters the other.
After the second division all four products are abnormal: two n+1 and two n−1.
Y is consistent with meiosis II nondisjunction in one first-division cell, giving n+1, n−1 and two normal n products.
Normal gametes have 3 chromosomes. X gives zygotes 7, 7, 5, 5; no zygote has 6.
Y gives 7, 5, 6, 6; half have the normal count.
Replication forms sister chromatids joined at each centromere; chromosome number is counted by centromeres rather than DNA strands or chromatids.

title: A crossover changes combinations rather than chromosome number
stem:
A replicated homologous pair contains four chromatids. The figure shows products of one reciprocal crossover between two non-sister chromatids. Colors A and B identify parental DNA regions, not different species. Chromatids 1 and 4 are unchanged; 2 and 3 contain exchanged terminal regions.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify which chromatids have new combinations of parental regions and calculate their fraction of this four-chromatid set.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the exchange can increase variation while preserving chromosome number and approximately preserving total DNA amount.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why independent orientation of this pair during meiosis I is a different source of variation and why mitosis normally preserves the parental cell’s ploidy.

steps.text: Chromatids 2 and 3 have exchanged regions; 1 and 4 remain parental combinations.
Two of four chromatids are recombinant, giving a fraction of 1/2.
Corresponding DNA regions are exchanged reciprocally between homologous non-sister chromatids, producing new combinations.
No centromere is added or removed, and corresponding lengths are swapped rather than copied into an extra chromosome.
Independent orientation changes which maternal/paternal homologues segregate together; crossing over changes combinations within chromatids.
Mitosis separates sister chromatids into daughter nuclei without a homolog-pair reduction division, preserving the chromosome-set number under normal conditions.

title: Absolute mass changes can hide the isotonic point
stem:
Plant-tissue pieces are placed in solutions with an impermeant solute. The initial/final masses are: 0.10 mol dm⁻³, 2.00/2.16 g; 0.20, 2.50/2.60 g; 0.40, 1.50/1.44 g; 0.50, 3.00/2.76 g. The graph shows percentage changes. Assume an approximately straight relationship between 0.20 and 0.40 mol dm⁻³. No formal test of differences is supplied.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage changes at 0.20 and 0.40 mol dm⁻³, then estimate the concentration at zero net mass change.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the changes using solute concentration and osmosis, and explain why zero net change does not mean water molecules stop moving.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Give two controls needed before interpreting the curve as a response to solution concentration.

steps.text: Use 100(final−initial)/initial rather than comparing raw gram changes.
At 0.20 the change is +4.00%; at 0.40 it is −4.00%.
Linear interpolation gives zero change at 0.300 mol dm⁻³.
Water enters tissue in the more dilute external solution and leaves in the more concentrated solution across partially permeable membranes.
At an isotonic point, opposing water movements balance; molecular exchange continues.
Use comparable tissue origin, dimensions/surface area and treatment time so biological and diffusion-path differences do not explain the response.
Standardize temperature and blotting before weighing; surface solution would otherwise change apparent mass without representing tissue uptake.

title: Equal initial particle concentrations need not give equal long-term cell volumes
stem:
Two external solutions have the same total dissolved-particle concentration as an animal cell’s initial contents. In model X the solute cannot cross the cell membrane. In model Y it crosses readily; the cell’s original solutes remain inside, and water can cross in both cases. The illustrated volume traces are observations. Ignore solute metabolism and active transport.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why X remains at approximately its initial volume while Y swells, despite equal initial total particle concentrations.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate Y’s percentage volume increase by minute 2 and explain why an animal cell is vulnerable to this response.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the graph establishes the identity of Y’s solute or predicts the exact time of lysis.

steps.text: In X the external solute remains outside, so the initially balanced osmotic conditions can persist.
In Y the permeant solute enters while original intracellular solutes remain, altering the effective osmotic balance.
Water then enters by osmosis; equal initial total concentration alone does not guarantee stable long-term tonicity.
An animal cell lacks a rigid cell wall that could develop opposing turgor pressure; excessive swelling can rupture its membrane.
The response is consistent with a permeant solute under the supplied assumptions, but multiple solutes can have that property.
The graph stops before any measured lysis event and supplies no membrane-failure threshold, so an exact lysis time cannot be deduced.

title: A hormone peak and a perturbation give different evidence
stem:
A constructed typical ovarian-cycle model has an LH surge near day 14 and a progesterone maximum near day 21. Estradiol rises before the LH surge. A treatment selectively prevents the LH surge while leaving the earlier follicular estradiol increase initially intact. Consider only the stated hormone pathway and its expected ovarian consequences.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how the earlier estradiol rise can be related to the LH surge, and how progesterone subsequently provides feedback.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Predict the effect of selectively suppressing the LH surge on ovulation and the later progesterone peak. Distinguish this prediction from an inference based only on the untreated graph.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the interval between the two stated maxima and explain why it is not a reliable universal calendar for all individuals.

steps.text: Sustained high estradiol before ovulation can exert positive feedback on the hypothalamic/pituitary pathway, promoting the LH surge.
LH promotes ovulation and corpus-luteum formation; subsequent progesterone contributes negative feedback that reduces further gonadotropin stimulation.
Ovulation is expected to be prevented or greatly reduced, with reduced corpus-luteum formation and a reduced later progesterone rise.
The untreated timing establishes an association; a selective perturbation provides stronger evidence about the role of LH in the pathway.
The model LH and progesterone maxima are separated by about 7 days.
Biological cycles vary between and within individuals; these constructed typical timings do not establish an identical timing for every cycle.

title: A pollination failure is not necessarily a lack of pollen
stem:
In a constructed experiment, self pollen, pollen from a closely related plant, or pollen from an unrelated compatible plant is placed on stigmas using equal pollen loads. Fruit set is 5%, 15% and 80% respectively. Bagged flowers receiving no pollen set no fruit. Plants are otherwise grown under the same conditions. One hundred treated flowers per group came from only one maternal plant.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare the evidence for pollen limitation and self-incompatibility. Give an additional observation that would help distinguish the mechanisms.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: For an equal group of 100 flowers, calculate the expected number setting fruit under the compatible cross-pollen treatment, and explain why this does not create 100 independent maternal-plant replicates.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Improve the design to test the population-level claim that compatible cross pollen increases fruit set.

steps.text: Equal applied pollen loads make a simple shortage of pollen an insufficient explanation for the low self-pollen fruit set.
Much greater fruit set with compatible cross pollen is consistent with a compatibility barrier, but fruit set alone does not identify its precise stage.
Observe pollen germination/tube growth or fertilization after each treatment to locate where self pollen fails.
Expected fruit-set count = 100 × 0.80 = 80 flowers.
Flowers on one maternal plant share genotype and maternal conditions; they are subsamples rather than 100 independent plants.
Use multiple independent maternal plants and randomly allocate matched flowers within each plant to each pollen treatment.
Include bagged no-pollen and handling controls, and record fruit set separately for each plant so plant-to-plant variation can be assessed.

title: A recessive child constrains both parental genotypes
stem:
In a fictional ABO family, one parent has phenotype A, the other B, and a child has phenotype O. Use alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i; assume ordinary Mendelian inheritance, no new mutation, and no rare modifiers of antigen expression. Each future conception is independent.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce both parental genotypes and explain the inference from the O phenotype.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct the four possible offspring genotypes and give the corresponding phenotype probabilities.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the probability that two future children include one O and one AB child, in either order. Explain why the existing O child does not force a different probability in the next conception.

steps.text: The O child is ii, so each parent supplied an i allele.
The parents must therefore be Iᴬi and Iᴮi under the stated model.
The four equally likely genotypes are IᴬIᴮ, Iᴬi, Iᴮi and ii.
AB, A, B and O phenotypes each have probability 1/4.
Include both orders: O then AB, or AB then O.
The earlier child establishes the parental genotype but does not alter independent allele segregation in subsequent conceptions.

title: An unaffected parent can carry a recessive X-linked allele
stem:
The fictional pedigree shows an unaffected mother and father, an affected son and an unaffected daughter. The condition is X-linked recessive with full penetrance; assume no new mutations. Write Xᴴ for the functional allele and Xʰ for the recessive allele. The father is XᴴY. Offspring sexes are equally likely in the probability model.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the mother’s genotype and explain why the unaffected daughter’s genotype is not fixed by her phenotype.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the probability that the next child is affected, and the probability that the next daughter, conditional on being a daughter, is a carrier.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that the affected son must have inherited the condition from his unaffected father.

steps.text: The son inherited Xʰ from his mother, so the unaffected mother must be XᴴXʰ.
The daughter receives Xᴴ from her father and can receive Xᴴ or Xʰ from her mother; both XᴴXᴴ and XᴴXʰ are unaffected.
An affected child must be a son receiving Xʰ: (1/2) × (1/2).
Probability the next child is affected = 1/4.
Among daughters, 1/2 are expected to be XᴴXʰ carriers.
The father supplies Y to a son in this model, not his X chromosome.
The son’s affected X-linked allele therefore came from the mother; absence of her affected phenotype does not imply absence of the allele.

title: A continuous phenotype does not separate genes from environment
stem:
Four plant genotypes are each cloned into two light treatments. Mean heights for genotypes 1–4 are 18, 20, 21, 25 cm in treatment L and 24, 29, 32, 31 cm in H. Clones within a genotype share the same inherited DNA sequence. A separate H-treatment box plot has Q1 = 26 cm and Q3 = 32 cm; use the supplied outlier rule, values below Q1−1.5IQR or above Q3+1.5IQR.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the treatment mean heights and percentage increase from L to H. Explain how the clones demonstrate phenotypic plasticity.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the supplied box-plot rule to decide whether 42 cm is an outlier. Explain why a statistical outlier is not automatically a measurement error.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether a continuous height distribution alone proves that many genes determine height.

steps.text: The same genotype gives different heights in the two environments, so environmental effects change phenotype without requiring a DNA-sequence change.
IQR = 6 cm; upper boundary = 32 + 1.5(6) = 41 cm, so 42 cm is an upper outlier.
An unusual value can reflect genuine biological variation; investigate measurement/procedure before deciding to exclude it.
Continuous variation is consistent with polygenic inheritance but can also be broadened by environmental differences.
The distribution alone does not partition genetic and environmental contributions; controlled breeding or common-environment evidence is required.

title: A feedback failure can occur at different points
stem:
The feedback diagram is incomplete because the return influence on insulin release is not drawn. Two constructed physiological models show persistently high blood glucose. Model A has very low insulin production; model B produces substantial insulin but target cells show reduced glucose uptake in response to the same supplied insulin concentration. Treat these as educational mechanisms, not individual clinical cases.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Complete the feedback explanation, identifying the controlled variable and the sign of the missing return influence.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare the likely sites of failure in A and B and relate them to the broad mechanisms of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A normal cell culture takes up 8.0 units of glucose with insulin and 2.0 without; model B cells take up 3.5 with and 2.0 without. Calculate insulin-stimulated increases and explain why comparing only the total uptake with insulin conceals useful information.

steps.text: Blood glucose concentration is the controlled variable.
As glucose falls toward the normal range, stimulation of beta cells and insulin release decrease; this opposes the original rise and is negative feedback.
A is consistent with failure of adequate insulin production, as in the insulin-deficiency mechanism of type 1 diabetes.
B is consistent with reduced target-cell responsiveness, a central mechanism of type 2 diabetes; insulin can be present while its effect is inadequate.
The insulin-stimulated increments are 6.0 units for normal cells and 1.5 for B, so B retains 25.0% of the normal increment.
Subtracting the no-insulin baseline isolates the additional response associated with insulin; total uptake includes both baseline and stimulated components.

title: Replica positions distinguish selection from need-directed mutation
stem:
A master plate contains bacterial colonies A–F grown before antibiotic exposure. Two replica plates receive cells from the same positions and contain antibiotic. Only colonies B and E grow on both replicas. Separate stored cells from B and E, taken from the master before any exposure, also grow when tested on antibiotic. Assume transfer positions are reliable.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the stored-master result is more informative than observing surviving colonies on a single antibiotic plate.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: In a separate mixture, 2 resistant and 98 susceptible cells are exposed. All resistant cells survive; 1% of susceptible cells survive. Calculate the expected resistant fraction among survivors.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the result does not mean every mutation is advantageous or that antibiotics deliberately choose an organism’s mutations.

steps.text: It shows that resistant cells existed in the relevant colonies before their first antibiotic exposure.
The recurring positions on replicas and the pre-exposure stored-cell test support selection of pre-existing heritable variation rather than production of a useful mutation only when needed.
Expected survivors are 2 resistant and 0.98 susceptible cells, total 2.98.
Resistant fraction = 2/2.98 = 0.671, or about 67.1%.
Fitness effects depend on the environment; resistant variants have a survival advantage under this drug treatment, while other mutations may be neutral or harmful.
The antibiotic is a selection pressure affecting differential survival, not a mechanism that designs a particular needed DNA change.

title: A mating advantage can be outweighed by predation
stem:
A constructed guppy model compares vivid and drab males. With no predation, a surviving vivid male averages four surviving offspring and a drab male two. Under a specified high-predation treatment, survival to breeding is 0.20 for vivid males and 0.80 for drab males. Offspring output per survivor is otherwise unchanged. Color has a heritable component, but environmental effects are also possible.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate expected offspring per initial male under high predation and identify which color has greater fitness by this measure.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how sexual selection and survival selection can act in opposite directions on the same trait.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why observing a color shift in one exposed group does not alone establish heritable evolutionary change.

steps.text: Multiply survival probability by offspring output conditional on survival.
Vivid: 0.20 × 4 = 0.80; drab: 0.80 × 2 = 1.60 offspring per initial male.
Drab males have twice the expected offspring output under this treatment despite vivid males’ mating advantage among survivors.
Mate choice can favor vivid males through greater reproductive success conditional on surviving.
Predation can favor drab males through a greater probability of reaching reproduction; net fitness includes both components.
The shift could include plastic color responses or changes in survival within one cohort; inheritance across generations must be demonstrated.
Compare descendants in a common environment or use breeding/genetic evidence to distinguish inherited differences from immediate environmental effects.

title: A bloom can precede oxygen loss rather than cause it by photosynthesis
stem:
Four independent nutrient-enriched pond mesocosms are followed over time. Constructed means at days 0, 4 and 8 are algal biomass 2, 8 and 4 relative units, and dissolved oxygen 8, 9 and 3 mg dm⁻³. In a separate dark five-day BOD test at fixed temperature, a water sample falls from 8.0 to 3.0 mg dm⁻³ oxygen, while a matched blank falls from 8.0 to 7.5. For this question, blank-corrected BOD is the sample oxygen decrease minus the blank decrease.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the sequence and explain a mechanism linking nutrient enrichment to later oxygen depletion.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate blank-corrected five-day BOD and explain why dark conditions matter.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify a limitation of attributing the field oxygen decline solely to the algal change from these means.

steps.text: Algal biomass first rises while oxygen remains high, then biomass declines while oxygen falls sharply.
Nutrients can increase primary production; subsequent dead biomass supports decomposers whose aerobic respiration increases oxygen demand.
Photosynthesis itself produces oxygen; a later decline is not explained by claiming that algal photosynthesis consumes oxygen.
Sample depletion is 5.0 and blank depletion 0.5 mg dm⁻³.
Corrected BOD = 4.5 mg dm⁻³ oxygen over five days.
Darkness prevents photosynthetic oxygen production from offsetting respiratory oxygen consumption during the test.
Temperature, mixing, gas exchange and other organismal respiration can also change oxygen; the time series alone does not isolate all causal contributions.

title: A one-year stock buffer is not a sustainable annual surplus
stem:
A model fish stock begins at 1000 tonnes. During one year, growth adds 150 tonnes, recruitment adds 200 and natural mortality removes 100. Harvest is additional. A habitat-management condition requires the end-of-year stock to remain at least 950 tonnes. For the first calculation, assume the supplied additions/losses are unaffected by harvest timing.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the largest harvest that maintains the initial stock, and the largest harvest satisfying only the stated one-year 950-tonne condition.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why harvesting 300 tonnes every year is not shown to be sustainable by these data.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State one ecological consideration that a biomass-only rule misses and one monitoring measure that would address it.

steps.text: Before harvest, stock is 1000 + 150 + 200 − 100 = 1250 tonnes.
Maintaining 1000 tonnes allows 250 tonnes harvest.
The one-year 950-tonne condition allows 300 tonnes.
The extra 50 tonnes uses standing stock rather than the annual net replacement; if the same budget were repeated it would reduce stock by 50 tonnes each year.
Growth, recruitment and mortality can also depend on stock size, age structure and environmental conditions, so the constant-budget assumption needs testing.
Equal total biomass can hide loss of reproductive adults or altered food-web effects; these can affect future recruitment and ecosystem function.
Monitor age/size structure, spawning abundance or dependent predator/prey populations as well as total biomass.

title: A factorial coral model separates two climate stresses
stem:
Six independent experimental tanks per treatment give constructed mean coral-calcification indices: control temperature/pH 100; warm only 70; lower pH only 80; both 40. No inferential test is supplied. A simple additive-loss model predicts the combined index by subtracting each separate loss from the control. Assume equal initial coral biomass and exposure duration.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the additive-loss prediction and compare it with the observed combined mean.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the biological distinction between warming-related bleaching and acidification-related suppression of calcification.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the four means alone establish a statistically significant interaction or inevitable reef collapse.

steps.text: Separate losses are 30 for warming and 20 for lower pH.
Additive prediction = 100 − 30 − 20 = 50; the observed combined mean is 40, ten units below this prediction.
High temperature can disrupt the coral–photosynthetic symbiont association, causing bleaching and loss of symbiont-derived resources.
Increased dissolved CO₂ lowers seawater pH and can suppress calcium-carbonate formation; this is distinct from loss of symbionts.
The means suggest a greater combined loss than the stated additive model, but variation and an appropriate interaction test are needed to assess statistical evidence.
Tank responses over a fixed interval do not alone establish every reef’s long-term outcome; ecological feedbacks, duration and recovery capacity also matter.

title: A replication fork constrains both strand directions
stem:
The figure represents prokaryotic DNA replication. The parental top strand runs 3′ to 5′ from left to right; the bottom runs 5′ to 3′. Fork progression is rightward. P is continuous newly synthesized DNA; Q contains separate fragments. In a separate linear Q region containing exactly four fragments, each begins with a 12-nucleotide RNA primer and initially contains 88 DNA nucleotides. Count only the internal joins between these four fragments.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the leading and lagging paths and explain why polymerase directionality produces the difference.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish the roles of primase, DNA polymerase III, DNA polymerase I and ligase in the stated prokaryotic system.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of RNA nucleotides replaced and the number of internal fragment joins sealed in the four-fragment region.

steps.text: P is leading and Q is lagging relative to the rightward fork.
DNA polymerase adds to a new strand’s 3′ end, so synthesis proceeds 5′ to 3′ while its template is read antiparallel.
The bottom template orientation requires repeated synthesis away from the moving fork, producing Okazaki fragments.
Primase supplies RNA primers; polymerase III extends the new DNA and can proofread its growing 3′ end.
Polymerase I removes/replaces RNA primer material with DNA; ligase seals remaining backbone nicks between adjacent DNA segments.
RNA replacement = 4 × 12 = 48 nucleotides; the final four-fragment region contains 4 × (12+88) = 400 DNA nucleotides.
There are three internal joins between four adjacent linear fragments, not four.

title: A proofreading error rate needs a defined DNA denominator
stem:
A bacterium’s chromosome has 4.00 × 10⁶ base pairs. In a constructed model, polymerase III makes an unrepaired mismatch with probability 10⁻⁶ per newly added nucleotide in wild type and 10⁻⁴ in a proofreading-defective mutant. Each daughter chromosome contains one new strand of 4.00 × 10⁶ nucleotides. Assume independent expected mismatch counts and ignore all other repair systems.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate expected mismatch counts for one daughter chromosome and for both daughter chromosomes in each model.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain what proofreading by polymerase III corrects and why its loss increases error rate without proving that every daughter cell has the mean number of errors.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that the 100-fold error increase must cause a 100-fold increase in harmful phenotypes.

steps.text: Multiply the number of newly added nucleotides per daughter by the stated mismatch probability.
Per daughter: wild type 4.00, mutant 400 expected mismatches; across both daughters: 8.00 and 800.
The two-strand parental base-pair count is not the number of newly added nucleotides in one daughter; the problem explicitly defines that denominator.
Polymerase III can remove a mismatched nucleotide at the growing 3′ end and replace it with a correctly paired nucleotide.
The calculation is an expectation over stochastic additions; actual daughter chromosomes can differ from the mean.
The mismatch probabilities differ by 10⁻⁴/10⁻⁶ = 100.
Many changes can be silent, occur outside a critical sequence or have context-dependent effects; phenotype does not scale directly with the count of DNA errors.

title: An exon can be skipped without shifting the reading frame
stem:
A gene region is transcribed into a pre-mRNA containing exons of 120, 90 and 150 nucleotides separated by introns of 80 and 110 nucleotides. Isoform A retains all three exons; B joins exon 1 directly to exon 3. Each isoform’s stated exon sequence runs from its start codon to and including its one final stop codon, with no untranslated regions in this model. Caps and poly(A) tails are excluded from the length counts. The exon joins preserve the reading frame.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate pre-mRNA length and the mature exon-sequence length of each isoform.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of amino acids in each product and explain why removing exon 2 does not necessarily cause a frameshift.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the products can still differ in function and why the two mRNAs do not imply two different inherited genes.

steps.text: Pre-mRNA length = 120+80+90+110+150 = 550 nucleotides.
A contains 360 exon nucleotides; B contains 270.
Divide the exon length by three and subtract the one stop codon, which encodes no amino acid.
A has 360/3−1 = 119 amino acids; B has 270/3−1 = 89.
The removed exon has 90 nucleotides, a whole number of codons, and the join is stated to preserve frame; the retained downstream codons need not shift.
The missing 30-amino-acid region may affect folding, an interaction surface or an active region even though the remaining frame is preserved.
Alternative RNA processing can produce different mRNAs/proteins from the same genomic gene; DNA sequence need not differ between the cells.

title: Ribosome sites distinguish transfer from translocation
stem:
The ribosome schematic has E, P and A sites. The P-site codon is GAA and the A-site codon UUU on mRNA read 5′ to 3′. The P-site tRNA carries a growing peptide ending in glutamate; the incoming A-site tRNA carries phenylalanine. Supplied pairing: GAA pairs with anticodon 3′-CUU-5′ and UUU with 3′-AAA-5′. A separate elongation model has 30 ribosomes, each advancing at four codons per second along a 180-codon coding segment; ignore initiation/termination times and stalls.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe peptide transfer and the subsequent site movements during one elongation step.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why anticodon orientation matters and predict an immediate effect of blocking entry of charged tRNAs to the A site.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Use the separate model to calculate traversal time for one ribosome and total amino-acid addition rate for all 30. Explain why 30 ribosomes need not mean 30 different genes.

steps.text: The growing chain is transferred from the P-site tRNA to the amino acid on the A-site tRNA, adding phenylalanine in this example.
Translocation shifts the peptidyl tRNA from A to P and the unloaded tRNA from P toward E, exposing the next codon at A.
Codon–anticodon pairing is complementary and antiparallel; the displayed 3′→5′ anticodons pair with 5′→3′ codons.
Blocking charged-tRNA entry prevents normal addition of the next amino acid, so elongation stalls rather than changing the DNA sequence.
Traversal time = 180/4 = 45.0 s; aggregate elongation = 30 × 4 = 120 amino acids s⁻¹.
Multiple ribosomes can translate the same mRNA, or mRNAs from the same gene; ribosome count does not identify distinct gene count.

title: A rescue experiment strengthens a gene-function inference
stem:
A constructed cell-culture experiment measures an enzyme-dependent product. Indices are wild type 100, a targeted edited line 20, the edited line plus a functional copy of the target gene 95, and a non-cutting Cas9/guide control 98. The edited line has a nine-base-pair deletion removing three catalytic-region codons. The deletion preserves the remaining reading frame. No detailed editing protocol is required.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the loss in the edited line relative to wild type and the fraction of that loss recovered by rescue.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the nine-base-pair deletion can impair function without being a frameshift, and how rescue supports the gene-function hypothesis.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State a role of the non-cutting control and one remaining limitation of a single edited line.

steps.text: The edited line loses 100−20 = 80 units, or 80.0% of wild-type product.
Rescue recovers 95−20 = 75 of the 80 lost units.
Recovered fraction = 75/80 = 93.75%.
Nine bases correspond to three complete codons, so the stated frame can remain intact while important catalytic-region amino acids are removed.
Restoring a functional target-gene copy substantially restores product, supporting a causal contribution of that gene rather than merely an association with editing treatment.
It helps test effects of the guide/Cas9 delivery or non-cutting treatment independently of the target DNA cut.
A single line can also carry other mutations or clonal differences; independently edited lines and sequence/off-target controls would strengthen the inference.

title: Sequence conservation and functional rescue test different claims
stem:
A candidate 120-nucleotide region differs at 12 aligned positions between two related species; a matched 120-nucleotide comparison region differs at 45. Alignment and mutation opportunity are assumed comparable. A knockout of the candidate gene reduces a cell function to 10% of control; supplying the other species’ gene restores it to 90%. The candidate sequence is not perfectly identical between species.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate divergence percentages and explain why greater conservation is evidence consistent with functional constraint rather than proof of it.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain what the knockout/rescue result adds to the sequence evidence.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the statements “all noncoding DNA is a neutral comparison” and “the rescued gene must have every function of the native gene”.

steps.text: Candidate divergence = 12/120 × 100 = 10.0%; comparison divergence = 45/120 × 100 = 37.5%.
Purifying selection can preserve functionally important sequence, but common ancestry, mutation-rate differences or the comparison choice can also affect conservation.
Loss of the gene reduces the measured function, and cross-species rescue restores much of it, supporting a conserved functional role in the tested cells.
This tests a functional prediction beyond sequence similarity alone; it does not require nucleotide identity at every position.
Noncoding DNA can include regulatory and structural functions and may itself be under selection; neutral status cannot simply be assumed from absence of coding.
One rescued assay demonstrates that tested function under those conditions, not every developmental, regulatory or environmental role of the native gene.

title: A 4C DNA peak is not a mitotic count
stem:
Five hundred cells from a proliferating tissue are classified by DNA amount: 250 at 2C, 150 between 2C and 4C, and 100 at 4C. Microscopy identifies 35 of the 4C cells as mitotic; the other 65 are in G2. In a separate treatment, 4C cells accumulate but the observed mitotic index falls. Assume comparable cell recovery and staining.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Assign the DNA-content groups to cell-cycle stages and calculate the mitotic index as a percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how a cell population can accumulate at 4C while fewer cells enter mitosis, relating the answer to regulation at a checkpoint.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why estimating cell-cycle speed from the mitotic index alone needs an additional assumption.

steps.text: The 2C group corresponds to G1; intermediate DNA amounts indicate S phase; the 4C group includes G2 and mitosis.
Mitotic index uses microscopically mitotic cells divided by all counted cells.
DNA replication can finish while entry into mitosis is delayed, causing G2 cells with 4C DNA to accumulate.
Failure to reach an appropriate cyclin-dependent regulatory threshold/checkpoint condition can prevent progression; a large DNA peak alone does not show rapid mitotic division.
A high fraction in mitosis can reflect a long mitotic duration or arrest, not just frequent entry; phase durations or time-resolved tracking are needed to infer proliferation rate.

title: One activated oncogene and two lost suppressor copies need different interpretations
stem:
In a constructed cultured-cell model, T is a functional tumor-suppressor allele and t inactive. O* is an activating oncogene variant. Under equal culture conditions, cells in mitosis are: TT/O 4 of 200; Tt/O 4 of 200; tt/O 40 of 200; TT/O* 30 of 200; tt/O* 100 of 200. These are snapshots, not direct measurements of cell-cycle duration or invasion.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate mitotic indices for tt/O and tt/O* and compare their ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the TT/Tt/tt pattern differs from the effect of O* in the stated model.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the highest index proves that those cells are malignant or divide 2.5 times as fast.

steps.text: The combined genotype’s snapshot index is 50/20 = 2.50 times the suppressor-loss-only index.
One functional T copy is sufficient for the low-index phenotype here; loss of both copies is associated with loss of suppressor restraint.
O* is associated with an increased index even when T remains functional, consistent with increased growth-promoting signaling rather than simple loss of a brake.
Malignancy requires evidence such as tissue invasion/metastatic behavior; mitotic index alone does not establish it.
The index is a phase fraction. Different mitotic dwell times or arrest can change it, so it is not automatically the same ratio as completed cell divisions per unit time.

title: A reporter experiment separates enhancer sequence from factor availability
stem:
A constructed reporter-gene assay gives relative mRNA levels: promoter alone with factor F present, 20; promoter plus enhancer with F, 100; promoter plus enhancer without F, 22; promoter plus mutated enhancer with F, 25. Corresponding protein levels are 40, 200, 44 and 50. Measurements use the same reporter coding sequence and comparable cell numbers. No particular named transcription factor is required.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the enhancer-associated mRNA fold change with F and its percentage increase over promoter alone.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the two additional comparisons support a sequence-specific regulatory interaction.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain what the mRNA/protein comparison adds and identify one conclusion the data do not establish.

steps.text: Fold change = 100/20 = 5.00-fold.
Percentage increase = (100−20)/20 × 100 = 400%, rather than a 500% increase.
Removing F largely removes the enhancer-associated increase, indicating that factor availability matters.
Mutating the enhancer also removes most of the increase despite F being present, consistent with a required DNA regulatory sequence and factor-mediated transcription.
Protein changes track mRNA changes at a constant protein:mRNA ratio of 2, supporting regulation upstream of protein production rather than only altered protein stability.
The assay does not by itself prove that F binds the enhancer directly; binding assays or other mechanistic evidence are needed to exclude indirect regulation.

title: mRNA lifetime can alter translation without altering transcription initiation
stem:
A transcription-blocking treatment is applied at time zero to two cell groups, each initially containing 100 molecules of a particular mRNA per average cell. The mRNA halves every 2.0 hours in control cells and every 4.0 hours with a stabilizing treatment. During the interval, each remaining mRNA produces two protein molecules per hour. Treat molecule counts as population means, assume no new transcription, and calculate instantaneous translation rates rather than accumulated protein.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine mRNA abundance after four hours and the corresponding instantaneous protein-production rate in each group.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how this is regulation of expression even though no new transcription occurs during the measurement.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that the final total protein must be exactly twice as large in the stabilized cells.

steps.text: Control mRNA = 25; stabilized mRNA = 50 molecules per average cell.
Multiply each remaining mRNA count by two protein molecules per mRNA per hour.
Rates at four hours are 50 and 100 protein molecules per average cell per hour.
Different mRNA degradation rates change the number of templates available to ribosomes.
A longer-lived transcript can sustain translation longer without changing the gene’s DNA sequence or requiring increased transcription initiation during the block.

The calculated ratio is of instantaneous production rates at four hours, not accumulated protein. Initial protein, time-dependent synthesis and protein degradation would also be needed for a total-protein comparison.

title: A persistent expression change can occur without a sequence change
stem:
A cloned cell population initially has four of five scored promoter cytosines methylated and relative mRNA abundance 20. A targeted demethylating treatment leaves one of five methylated and mRNA abundance 80. The promoter base sequence remains unchanged. The altered tag pattern and expression persist through two mitotic passages after treatment removal. A vehicle-treated clone retains the original pattern.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate promoter methylation percentages and the mRNA fold change, then explain the relationship to transcriptional control.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the result is an example of an epigenetic change and what the passages add to the evidence.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claims that this proves inheritance through gametes and that histone methylation always has the same transcriptional effect as promoter methylation.

steps.text: Methylation changes from 4/5 = 80% to 1/5 = 20%; mRNA increases fourfold.
Promoter cytosine methylation can repress downstream transcription; removing these tags is consistent with increased expression in the tested cells.
The expression/tag pattern changes without alteration of the DNA base sequence, distinguishing it from a sequence mutation.
Persistence through mitotic passages supports transmission of the expression state to daughter cells beyond the immediate treatment exposure.
Mitotic persistence in this cell culture does not establish transmission through meiosis or offspring; many gametic epigenetic tags are reset.
Histone methylation can activate or repress transcription depending on context; its effect must not be generalized from this promoter-cytosine result.

title: A pressure term can reverse a solute-only prediction
stem:
Three plant cells are in contact with an external solution of water potential −250 kPa. Cell A has Ψs = −600 and Ψp = +400 kPa; B has −450 and +100; C has −300 and 0. Use Ψw = Ψs + Ψp. All values use the same reference and temperature. For a short model adjustment of B only, assume its solute component remains fixed while pressure changes.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate each cell’s total water potential and predict initial net water movement relative to the external solution.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: For the stated short adjustment of B, calculate the pressure potential at equilibrium with the external solution.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why A disproves a prediction based only on comparing solute concentration and state a limitation of treating B’s solute component as fixed.

steps.text: A: −200 kPa; B: −350 kPa; C: −300 kPa.
Water moves from higher to lower water potential: initially out of A, into B and into C.
Set −250 = −450 + Ψp while retaining the stipulated fixed solute component.
Ψp = +200 kPa.
A’s positive pressure raises its total above the external value despite its more negative solute potential, so initial water movement is outward.
Real water entry changes cell volume and can dilute solutes; Ψs need not remain constant during a large adjustment. The computed pressure applies to the stated limited model.

title: At incipient plasmolysis the pressure component is zero
stem:
A fresh plant cell has Ψs = −600 kPa and Ψp = +400 kPa. After equilibration in an external solution of Ψw = −750 kPa, it is just at incipient plasmolysis, where turgor pressure is zero. For a supplied ideal fixed-temperature model, solute amount is conserved and Ψs is inversely proportional to protoplast volume. The cell sketches are schematic and do not encode a volume scale.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the initial total water potential and the final solute potential at the stated plasmolysis point.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the supplied inverse-volume model to calculate final protoplast volume as a fraction of its initial value and the percentage decrease.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the initial movement and evaluate assigning pressure potential −750 kPa to the plasmolyzed cell.

steps.text: Initially Ψw = −600 + 400 = −200 kPa.
At equilibrium Ψw = −750 kPa and Ψp = 0, so final Ψs = −750 kPa.
With conserved solute amount at fixed temperature, Ψs,initial × Vinitial = Ψs,final × Vfinal.
Vfinal/Vinitial = (−600)/(−750) = 0.800; volume decreases by 20.0%.
The initial cell total −200 kPa exceeds external −750 kPa, so water initially leaves; solutes become more concentrated as protoplast volume falls.
At the stipulated incipient plasmolysis point the pressure term is zero, not the negative external total; assigning −750 to Ψp confuses separate components.

For counting only, assume each primary oocyte ultimately yields one functional ovum and three recovered polar-body products; each primary spermatocyte yields four functional sperm. All start after replication at DNA content 4C, and each final haploid product contains 1C. The diagram represents relative cytoplasmic allocation, not a calibrated volume.

title: Sperm entry and normal ploidy need different denominators
stem:
In a constructed gamete study, control oocytes show at least one sperm entry in 80% of oocytes; 5% of those entered oocytes are polyspermic. With an acrosome inhibitor, entry is 10% and polyspermy among entered oocytes 4%. With a cortical-reaction inhibitor, entry is 78% and polyspermy among entered oocytes 45%. Assume a single-sperm entry would otherwise produce the normal diploid zygote and ignore later viability.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

steps.text: Multiply entry probability by the fraction of entered oocytes with only one sperm.
Control = 0.80 × 0.95 = 0.760, or 76.0% of original oocytes.
Cortical-inhibitor group = 0.78 × 0.55 = 0.429, or 42.9%.
The acrosomal reaction helps sperm penetrate egg-associated layers; its inhibition strongly reduces entry.
The cortical reaction helps prevent additional sperm entry after the first; inhibiting it can leave initial entry high while greatly increasing polyspermy.
That compares entry alone and ignores the conditional polyspermy proportion; the normal single-sperm outcome is substantially reduced.
Multiple sperm can introduce extra chromosome sets, so entry is not equivalent to normal fertilization and ploidy.

title: Placental exchange does not require the blood circuits to mix
stem:
A constructed placental-exchange model has maternal and fetal blood separated by a thin villous barrier. Oxygen partial pressures are 80 and 30 relative pressure units in maternal/fetal blood; carbon dioxide partial pressures are 40 and 50. For a supplied diffusion model, flux is proportional to surface area × partial-pressure difference / barrier thickness. A structural change doubles area and halves thickness; the pressure differences are initially unchanged.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Predict initial net movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide and relate the answer to partial-pressure gradients.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the predicted flux multiplier after the stated structural change and explain why this does not mean real flux can increase indefinitely.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why fetal and maternal red blood cells need not cross the barrier for gas exchange, and identify which fetal umbilical vessel carries blood returning from the placenta toward the fetus.

steps.text: Oxygen moves from maternal to fetal blood; carbon dioxide moves from fetal to maternal blood.
Each gas initially diffuses from its higher to lower partial pressure across the exchange barrier.
The area factor is 2 and inverse-thickness factor is 1/0.5.
Predicted flux increases fourfold while the stated gradients remain unchanged.
Real blood supply, gas delivery and changing gradients can become limiting; the proportional model isolates only the stated structural factors.
Gas molecules cross the barrier while the blood circuits remain distinct; wholesale blood-cell mixing is not required.
The umbilical vein carries blood from the placenta toward the fetus, relatively oxygenated compared with the umbilical arteries going to the placenta.

Observed phenotype counts for A_B_, A_bb, aaB_ and aabb are 180, 65, 55 and 20, total 320. Use χ² = Σ(O−E)²/E and, for this four-category comparison with no parameters fitted, three degrees of freedom. The supplied 5% critical value is 7.815.

title: A recombination fraction is not automatically a fraction of meioses
stem:
A heterozygous parent has linked alleles AB/ab as shown and is testcrossed to ab/ab. Offspring reflect gametes AB 410, ab 390, Ab 110 and aB 90. Assume equal viability and reliable scoring. For the final model only, suppose every relevant meiosis has either no crossover or exactly one crossover between the loci, and one crossover makes two of four chromatids recombinant.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify parental and recombinant classes and calculate the recombination fraction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Under the supplied single-crossover model, calculate the fraction of meioses that had a crossover in the interval.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain one reason the conversion from 20% to 40% would not be justified without the extra assumptions.

steps.text: AB and ab are parental classes; Ab and aB are recombinant.
Use both recombinant classes divided by all offspring.
Recombination fraction = (110+90)/1000 = 0.200, or 20.0%.
A crossover meiosis contributes recombinant chromatids in only half its products.
If half the products of fraction f of meioses are recombinant, 0.5f = 0.20 and f = 0.40, or 40.0%.
Multiple crossovers can restore parental marker combinations, and chromatid sampling/viability can also affect observed offspring classes.
Thus a recombinant-offspring fraction does not universally measure the same fraction of meiotic events; the relationship depends on the specified crossover model.

title: Renal amounts require both concentration and flow
stem:
An inert marker is freely filtered by a model kidney and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted. Plasma marker concentration is 0.020 mg mL⁻¹, urine concentration 2.40 mg mL⁻¹ and urine flow 1.00 mL min⁻¹. Use filtered marker amount per minute = excreted marker amount per minute. Plasma urea is 5.00 mmol dm⁻³ and urine urea 300 mmol dm⁻³. For urea only, assume no secretion or production in the nephron.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate glomerular filtration rate from the marker data, including units.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate filtered and excreted urea per minute, then its net reabsorbed fraction under the stated assumptions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a urine urea concentration much greater than plasma does not by itself prove secretion of urea into the nephron.

steps.text: Excreted marker = 2.40 mg mL⁻¹ × 1.00 mL min⁻¹ = 2.40 mg min⁻¹.
Filtration rate = 2.40 mg min⁻¹ / 0.020 mg mL⁻¹ = 120 mL min⁻¹ = 0.120 dm³ min⁻¹.
Filtered urea = 5.00 × 0.120 = 0.600 mmol min⁻¹; excreted = 300 × 0.00100 = 0.300 mmol min⁻¹.
Net reabsorbed urea = 0.300 mmol min⁻¹, or 50.0% of the filtered amount.
Reabsorption of water can concentrate the urea remaining in the tubule even while some urea is reabsorbed.
Amount flux, not concentration alone, determines the balance; the urine flow is far below the filtration flow in this model.

title: ADH changes water permeability rather than pumping water
stem:
A constructed collecting-duct model has urine flow 1.00 mL min⁻¹ and osmolar concentration 1600 milliosmoles dm⁻³ with high ADH, compared with 8.00 mL min⁻¹ and 200 milliosmoles dm⁻³ with low ADH. Treat osmolar concentration as dissolved-particle amount per volume for this calculation. A second manipulation prevents normal sodium transport by the ascending limb and reduces the medullary gradient despite high ADH.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate urine volume and dissolved-particle amount excreted in 30 minutes in each ADH condition.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how ADH can change volume/concentration without changing this particle-excretion load.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why high ADH alone does not restore the original urine concentration when the medullary gradient is reduced.

steps.text: Volumes are 30.0 mL = 0.0300 dm³ with high ADH and 240 mL = 0.240 dm³ with low ADH.
Multiply each volume by its osmolar concentration in matching volume units.
Both excrete 48.0 milliosmoles: 0.0300 × 1600 and 0.240 × 200.
ADH increases aquaporin-mediated collecting-duct water permeability, allowing more water reabsorption along the medullary osmotic gradient.
Water is moving by osmosis rather than being actively pumped by ADH; less remaining water concentrates the excreted particles.
Increased permeability requires an appropriate water-potential gradient to drive reabsorption.
Ascending-limb sodium transport contributes to that medullary gradient; weakening it can reduce water removal even when collecting ducts contain aquaporins.

title: Selection survivors need not already be in Hardy–Weinberg proportions
stem:
An initial model population contains AA 490, Aa 420 and aa 90 individuals. Viability to breeding is 1.00, 0.80 and 0.20 respectively; ignore other fitness differences and migration. All surviving breeders then mate randomly in a very large population, with ordinary segregation and no new mutation. Use p+q=1 and p²:2pq:q² for the next zygote generation under those assumptions.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate surviving genotype counts and the new a-allele frequency among breeders.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the aa fraction among the next zygotes and explain why 18/844 is not the Hardy–Weinberg prediction for them.

steps.text: q = 0.300 and p = 0.700; expected genotype fractions are 0.49, 0.42 and 0.09, matching the initial counts.
Survivors: AA 490, Aa 336, aa 18; total 844.
Count a copies in survivors and divide by twice all surviving individuals.

title: Similar population means can hide different selection patterns
stem:
Three constructed environments have the illustrated survival probabilities across a heritable quantitative trait. S1 favors intermediate values; S2 increases survival toward larger values; S3 favors both extremes over intermediate values. At trait values 2 and 5, S1 survival probabilities are 0.640 and 1.00. Assume equal reproduction among survivors when comparing this component of fitness.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the selection pattern in each environment and compare the predicted effect on trait variation.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the relative survival advantage of trait 5 over trait 2 under S1, expressed as a percentage increase relative to trait 2.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claims that an unchanged mean proves no selection occurred and that disruptive selection proves new species have formed.

steps.text: S1 is stabilizing, S2 directional toward larger trait values, and S3 disruptive.
S1 tends to reduce extreme values; S2 shifts favored values toward one side; S3 favors both tails and can maintain/increase separation of trait classes.
Compare the difference with the trait-2 baseline: (1.00−0.640)/0.640.
Relative increase = 56.25%; this differs from the 36-percentage-point probability difference.
Opposite changes in extremes or reduced variation can leave a similar mean, so the distribution and fitness pattern matter.
Disruptive survival differences alone do not demonstrate reproductive isolation or separate species; mating patterns and divergence evidence are needed.

title: A breeding response is not a percentage of height caused by genes
stem:
A constructed plant-breeding study begins with mean height 20.0 cm. Breeders deliberately select parents averaging 30.0 cm. Their offspring, grown in a common environment, average 22.0 cm, while offspring of randomly selected control parents average 20.0 cm. Separately, extra nutrient supply makes clones average 30.0 cm, but their untreated descendants average 20.0 cm. For one descriptive ratio, divide the offspring response above control by the selected-parent difference above the initial mean.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the descriptive response ratio using the supplied definition.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the selected-offspring comparison supports an inherited response more strongly than the nutrient-treated clone comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that the 0.200 ratio means exactly 20% of every plant’s height is genetic. Distinguish deliberate breeding from incidental antibiotic selection.

steps.text: Offspring response = 22−20 = 2 cm; selected-parent difference = 30−20 = 10 cm.
Response ratio = 2/10 = 0.200.
Selected-parent descendants remain taller than control descendants in a common environment, consistent with inherited differences associated with deliberate breeding.

Nutrient-treated clones change height, but their untreated descendants return to control height; that pattern is consistent with a direct environmental response rather than the demonstrated inherited response.
This is a response-to-selection ratio for a specified population/environment; it does not divide an individual’s height into genetic and environmental centimeter portions or identify one causal gene.

Breeders intentionally choose reproducing plants, an artificial-selection process. Unintended antibiotic resistance reflects natural selection under a human-created pressure, rather than intentional choice of resistant organisms for breeding.

title: A chronosequence is a hypothesis about time built from space
stem:
Four substrate-age classes in a constructed primary-succession study are 0, 20, 60 and 120 years. Mean plant biomass indices are 0, 4, 18 and 35; mean soil-nitrogen indices are 0.2, 1.0, 3.0 and 5.0. Different sites represent the ages, with four independent sites in each class. The sites have broadly comparable climate but may differ in initial rock chemistry and dispersal access.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain two mechanisms by which early colonists can facilitate later plant establishment.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the biomass increase from age 20 to 120 as a percentage of age-20 biomass and compare it with the nitrogen-index change over that interval.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that every age-20 site will necessarily have index 35 after exactly 100 further years.

steps.text: Colonists can contribute organic matter and promote soil development, improving water retention and rooting conditions.
Changes to nutrient availability and local microclimate can make the initially bare substrate suitable for additional species.
Biomass increase = (35−4)/4 × 100 = 775%.
Nitrogen index increases from 1.0 to 5.0, a 400% increase; different relative changes do not establish a fixed causal proportionality.
A space-for-time comparison assumes sites are otherwise comparable; initial substrate, dispersal and disturbance differences can change trajectories.
The means are not a time-resolved fate for every individual site, and succession can be arrested, disturbed or follow alternative pathways.

title: Removing a disturbance can release arrested succession
stem:
In a constructed restoration experiment, six independent landscape blocks each contain randomly assigned plots in a two-factor design. After ten years, mean shrub cover is 20% with grazing/no seed addition, 25% with grazing/seed addition, 60% with grazing exclusion/no seeds and 70% with exclusion/seed addition. Initial cover is comparable at about 15%. No inferential statistical test is supplied.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the grazing-exclusion effect within each seed treatment and the seed-addition effect within each grazing treatment.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the results can support arrested succession rather than an abiotic inability of the site to support shrubs.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the strength and limit of the causal interpretation.

steps.text: Exclusion raises cover by 40 percentage points without seeds and by 45 with seeds.
Seed addition raises cover by 5 points under grazing and by 10 under exclusion.
Shrubs establish much more extensively when grazing is excluded, even without added seeds, so continued disturbance can hold back later vegetation stages.
Existing-site conditions allow shrub establishment under the exclusion treatment; grazing can therefore maintain an earlier community rather than the site being intrinsically incapable of change.
Random assignment within independent blocks and a seed factor help isolate effects from initial location differences and seed limitation.
Means alone do not establish statistical significance or a universal endpoint; assess block variation, replicate consistency and longer-term outcomes before extending the claim.

title: A stable regional mosaic can contain changing patches
stem:
Six equally sized habitat patches are surveyed at years 0, 10 and 20. The figure records early (E), middle (M) and late (L) community stages. All three stages remain represented in two patches at each survey, but individual patches change. Local disturbance and vegetation feedbacks allow stages to recur rather than following one irreversible region-wide sequence.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the late-stage fraction at each survey and determine whether the same patches remain late throughout.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how this illustrates stability at one spatial scale and succession at another.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify a limitation of the ten-year sampling interval and a measurement that would improve interpretation.

steps.text: Each survey has 2/6 = 1/3, or about 33.3%, late-stage area.
No patch remains L at all three surveys; unchanged regional proportion does not mean unchanged patch identity.
The region maintains a similar distribution of stages while local patch communities change over time.
Cyclical or recurrent succession can maintain a shifting mosaic; stability need not mean no biological change or one permanent climax everywhere.
Unobserved changes between surveys could include additional transitions or different transition sequences; three snapshots do not reconstruct every pathway.
Use more frequent permanent-patch surveys with disturbance, species and environmental records to test proposed cycles rather than inferring them only from stage labels.

title: Small shifts in hatching need not track a large shift in prey
stem:
A constructed great-tit/caterpillar model compares a cool and a warm spring. Caterpillar peak biomass occurs on year-days 140 and 125 respectively; chick hatching occurs on days 135 and 132. Peak chick food demand occurs seven days after hatching. In this model, caterpillar timing responds strongly to spring temperature, whereas bird breeding timing responds partly to photoperiod. These illustrative values are not a reported field dataset.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate absolute mismatch between peak prey and peak chick demand in each spring and the increase in mismatch.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the different environmental cues can produce this result and predict one possible effect on chick performance.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claims that an earlier breeding date proves evolutionary adaptation and that warming always improves synchrony.

steps.text: Cool: demand day 142 and prey day 140, mismatch 2 days. Warm: demand day 139 and prey day 125, mismatch 14 days.
Mismatch increases by 12 days even though hatching itself advances by 3 days.
Temperature-driven prey development can advance more than bird breeding if the latter remains constrained by photoperiod or other cues.
Peak chick demand can then occur after prey biomass declines, potentially reducing food delivery, growth or survival.
A timing shift can be plastic or demographic; heritable change across generations requires inheritance/selection evidence, not just different dates.
The calculated example shows reduced synchrony despite earlier hatching; the relative responses of interacting species matter rather than a shared direction of change alone.

title: A fractional generation cannot be rounded into another complete life cycle
stem:
For a supplied spruce-bark-beetle development model, accumulated degree-days are (mean temperature−10 °C) × season days when temperature exceeds 10 °C. Each complete generation requires 300 degree-days, with no carryover into the next year. Compare seasons: X = 120 days at 15.0 °C; Y = 120 days at 16.5 °C; Z = 150 days at 18.0 °C. For a separate unconstrained population illustration, each completed generation multiplies numbers by three.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate degree-days and complete generations in each season.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the separate multiplication model to compare population factors after the complete generations in X and Z.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain two limitations of using these calculations as a precise prediction of a real outbreak.

steps.text: X: 600 degree-days, two complete generations; Y: 780, two complete generations plus partial development; Z: 1200, four complete generations.
780/300 = 2.6 does not represent three completed generations under the stated threshold and no-carryover model.
Use 3² for X and 3⁴ for Z, applying only complete generations.
Population factors are 9 and 81; Z’s factor is nine times X’s.
Real temperatures fluctuate and developmental thresholds, mortality and overwintering can differ from the supplied constant-temperature/no-carryover assumptions.
Host supply, competition, predation and disease can limit multiplication, so a constant threefold increase per generation is not an unlimited real-population forecast.

title: Climate-related survival can change morph frequencies without revealing allele frequencies
stem:
Two matched tawny-owl model cohorts each start with 100 brown and 300 gray individuals. In a snowy-winter treatment, survival is 0.40 for brown and 0.80 for gray; in a low-snow treatment it is 0.90 and 0.75. Assume no migration and equal reproduction after survival. Color has a heritable component, but the exact genetic architecture and dominance are not given. The values are constructed to explore a hypothesis about climate-related fitness.

All datasets and schematics in this question are constructed for practice. Give numerical answers with appropriate units and precision.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the brown-morph frequency among survivors in each treatment and compare it with the initial frequency.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain what would be required for the survival difference to produce evolutionary change in the population.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the brown-morph frequency can be inserted directly as q in a Hardy–Weinberg calculation.

steps.text: Initial frequency is 100/400 = 0.250; use each treatment’s surviving total as the new denominator.
Brown frequency decreases under snowy conditions but increases under the specified low-snow relative-survival pattern.
The relevant color variation must be heritable and survivors must contribute differentially to subsequent generations.
With these conditions and the stated absence of migration, altered relative fitness can change the inherited variant distribution over generations.
A phenotype frequency is not automatically an allele frequency. Dominance, number of loci and genotype–phenotype relationships are not supplied.
Additional inheritance/genotype information is required before using the morph proportion as an allele frequency or assigning a recessive q² interpretation.
